rationale: The exact entry's identification is directly established by the three printed proof-texts (Isa 8:7 explicitly equates the rising waters with the king of Assyria and his host; Jer 47:2 equates the overflowing flood from the north with an invading army that overflows land and city; Dan 9:26 places the end 'with a flood' in a context of military desolation). The chapter supplies the consistent cross-text pattern (floods/waters as peoples or armies in motion, including the Lord's host as the reverse flood) that makes the same identification hold uniformly. No material assertion printed in the entry is left unsupported, and no rival reading accounts for the same explicit equations and parallel columns with equal or greater precision.
book_core_identification: Flood = destroying waters that are peoples in motion (specifically an invading nation or the Lord's own host sweeping the enemy away).
chapter_only_objections: The chapter's reversed reading of the singular verb and subject in Dan 9:26 (Messiah's host as the flood that destroys the prince's people) is an extended argument not asserted in the glossary entry itself.

Extended typological mappings (Red Sea as rehearsal of Babylon's fall, witnesses' power to turn waters to blood as authority to kill peoples, sea-of-glass as stilled heavenly assembly, etc.) go beyond the entry's scope.
The claim that roughly three-fourths of all sea/waters occurrences are symbolic rather than geographic is a chapter-level statistical assertion.
strongest_counter_interpretation: In the cited prophetic texts, 'flood' is simply vivid metaphor or stock imagery for overwhelming military disaster or divine judgment, without any fixed, transferable symbolic identification of the waters themselves as 'peoples in motion'.
counter_core_identification: Flood language = general poetic figure for catastrophic invasion or judgment, not a defined symbol whose referent is peoples/armies.
material_core_denial: The counter denies that the waters/flood are themselves the peoples or host; it treats the equation as disposable imagery rather than Scripture's own consistent definition.
counter_case: Isa 8:7 and Jer 47:2 can be read as similes ('like waters') rather than identifications.
Dan 9:26's 'flood' can be taken as ordinary idiom for the intensity of the war's end without requiring a people-as-water referent.
Many other flood texts (Noah, Psalms of distress) function without any 'peoples in motion' sense, suggesting the image is flexible rather than fixed.
book_explanatory_advantages: Accounts for the explicit appositions in the printed proof-texts (waters = king of Assyria; flood = army from the north) without remainder.

Unifies the same image across independent witnesses (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Daniel, Revelation's dragon-flood, Egypt rising 'as a flood') via Hebrew parallel columns that repeatedly set seas/waters against peoples/nations.
Explains both directions of the motion (hostile invasion and the Lord's reverse host) from the same definition, matching the entry's wording exactly.
Preserves the literal military events while showing why water imagery is chosen.
counter_explanatory_advantages: Requires no commitment to a system-wide symbolic lexicon.
Fits ordinary English usage of 'flood' as hyperbole for any overwhelming force.
decisive_sources: Isaiah 8:7 (waters of the river = king of Assyria and all his glory)
Jeremiah 47:2 (waters from the north = overflowing flood that overflows land and city)
Daniel 9:26 (end with a flood in context of war and desolation)
Chapter's parallel-column citations (Isa 17:12-13; Ps 65:7; Luke 21:25) establishing waters = peoples
